title: NLP Prediction, Vision Modeling & Clustering: AI Across Data Types
summary: Machine learning is not limited to numbers in a spreadsheet. Text, images and unlabeled data all carry patterns a model can learn from. Terms covered: - NLP Prediction: making predictions from text rather than generating it. Routing support tickets by urgency, classifying sentiment in financial news, flagging patients at elevated risk from clinical notes. - Vision Modeling: the same principle applied to images and video. Detecting production line defects in milliseconds, identifying anomalies in medical scans, tracking infrastructure change from satellite imagery. - Clustering: finding natural groupings based on similarity with no predefined categories. The model does not classify, it discovers. Text, images and unlabeled data. Three very different inputs, made meaningful through the same underlying capability. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #MachineLearning #ComputerVision #Clustering #AIGlossary #H2Oai
summary_html:
Machine learning is not limited to numbers in a spreadsheet. Text, images and unlabeled data all carry patterns a model can learn from.

Terms covered:
- NLP Prediction: making predictions from text rather than generating it. Routing support tickets by urgency, classifying sentiment in financial news, flagging patients at elevated risk from clinical notes.
- Vision Modeling: the same principle applied to images and video. Detecting production line defects in milliseconds, identifying anomalies in medical scans, tracking infrastructure change from satellite imagery.
- Clustering: finding natural groupings based on similarity with no predefined categories. The model does not classify, it discovers.

Text, images and unlabeled data. Three very different inputs, made meaningful through the same underlying capability.

—

title: India Non Smartphone Electronics Exports Hit $13.79 Billion Up 56.5% #Shorts #FrontPage
summary: Government figures put India's non smartphone electronics exports at $13.79 billion, an increase of 56.5%, lifting their share of electronics exports to about 43%. title: MiniMax H3 Image - Normal + GGUF Guide!
summary: MiniMax just released H3-Image, a new open image model that can render insanely detailed images at up to 16+ megapixels. In this video, I'll show you how to run it locally in ComfyUI. We'll go through which model files to download, the right settings, and how to get the best quality out of it. Let's get started. ### MiniMax H3-Image in ComfyUI – Links & Requirements ### MODELS - Official ComfyUI files (int8, w4a8, text encoders, VAE, PE): https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3-Image/tree/main - GGUF models by Abiray (for low VRAM): https://huggingface.co/Abiray/MiniMax-H3-Image-GGUF - Abiray's GGUF workflow (drag into ComfyUI): https://huggingface.co/Abiray/MiniMax-H3-Image-GGUF/resolve/main/image_minimax_h3_image_t2i_gguf.json - GGUF fix script (place directly in ComfyUI/custom_nodes, then restart): https://huggingface.co/Abiray/MiniMax-H3-Image-GGUF/blob/main/minimax_h3_image_gguf_fix.py REQUIREMENTS - ComfyUI version 0.45.0 or newer (older versions don't know the "minimax" model type). - For GGUF: the ComfyUI-GGUF custom node by city96, updated to the latest version. - PyTorch / CUDA: no official minimum has been published. A current ComfyUI Portable build (e.g. PyTorch 2.13 with CUDA 13.0) works on RTX 40-series cards. - GTX 10-series (Pascal) cards: use the ComfyUI Portable build with CUDA 12.6 and GGUF models only. - NVIDIA driver: CUDA 13.x requires driver 580 or newer. HOW TO CHECK YOUR VERSIONS 1. PyTorch and CUDA (ComfyUI Portable): Open a command prompt in the ComfyUI_windows_portable folder and run: python_embeded\python.exe -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.is_available())" Example output: 2.13.0+cu130 13.0 True (PyTorch version, CUDA version PyTorch was built with, GPU detected) 2. Driver and max supported CUDA version: Run nvidia-smi and look at "CUDA Version" in the top right. 3. ComfyUI and PyTorch version are also shown at the top of the ComfyUI startup log ("ComfyUI version:" and "pytorch version:"). RECOMMENDED SETTINGS - Steps: 6, CFG: 1, Sampler: euler, Scheduler: simple, no negative prompt. - Resolution: the model works best between 4 and 20 megapixels (ideal ~16 MP, e.g. 4096x4096). Use at least 2048x2048 (4 MP). - VAE: minimax_h3_image_vae_fp16.safetensors (24-channel). Do not use SD, Flux or video VAEs. #### Join and Support me #### Buy me a Coffee: https://www.buymeacoffee.com/oliviotutorials Joint my Discord Group: https://discord.gg/XKAk7GUzAW Support me on Patreon: https://www.patreon.com/sarikas 00:00 Intro 00:21 Sampler IMages MiniMax H3 04:14 ComfyUI MiniMax H3 Image Guide 09:54 GGUF MiniMax H3 Image by Abiray 13:15 Comfy Org Cloud Render
summary_html:
MiniMax just released H3-Image, a new open image model that can render insanely detailed images at up to 16+ megapixels. 

In this video, I'll show you how to run it locally in ComfyUI. We'll go through which model files to download, the right settings, and how to get the best quality out of it. Let's get started.

### MiniMax H3-Image in ComfyUI – Links & Requirements ###

MODELS
- Official ComfyUI files (int8, w4a8, text encoders, VAE, PE):
  https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3-Image/tree/main
- GGUF models by Abiray (for low VRAM):
  https://huggingface.co/Abiray/MiniMax-H3-Image-GGUF
- Abiray's GGUF workflow (drag into ComfyUI):
  https://huggingface.co/Abiray/MiniMax-H3-Image-GGUF/resolve/main/image_minimax_h3_image_t2i_gguf.json
- GGUF fix script (place directly in ComfyUI/custom_nodes, then restart):
  https://huggingface.co/Abiray/MiniMax-H3-Image-GGUF/blob/main/minimax_h3_image_gguf_fix.py

REQUIREMENTS
- ComfyUI version 0.45.0 or newer (older versions don't know the "minimax" model type).
- For GGUF: the ComfyUI-GGUF custom node by city96, updated to the latest version.
- PyTorch / CUDA: no official minimum has been published. A current ComfyUI Portable build
  (e.g. PyTorch 2.13 with CUDA 13.0) works on RTX 40-series cards.
- GTX 10-series (Pascal) cards: use the ComfyUI Portable build with CUDA 12.6 and GGUF models only.
- NVIDIA driver: CUDA 13.x requires driver 580 or newer.

HOW TO CHECK YOUR VERSIONS
1. PyTorch and CUDA (ComfyUI Portable):
   Open a command prompt in the ComfyUI_windows_portable folder and run:
   python_embeded\python.exe -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.is_available())"
   Example output: 2.13.0+cu130 13.0 True
   (PyTorch version, CUDA version PyTorch was built with, GPU detected)
2. Driver and max supported CUDA version:
   Run nvidia-smi and look at "CUDA Version" in the top right.
3. ComfyUI and PyTorch version are also shown at the top of the ComfyUI startup log
   ("ComfyUI version:" and "pytorch version:").

RECOMMENDED SETTINGS
- Steps: 6, CFG: 1, Sampler: euler, Scheduler: simple, no negative prompt.
- Resolution: the model works best between 4 and 20 megapixels (ideal ~16 MP, e.g. 4096x4096).
  Use at least 2048x2048 (4 MP).
- VAE: minimax_h3_image_vae_fp16.safetensors (24-channel). Do not use SD, Flux or video VAEs.

title: Deep Learning, Transformers & Neural Networks: How Modern AI Learns
summary: Modern AI did not come from traditional programming. It came from a series of architectural breakthroughs, and three terms trace the whole path. Terms covered: - Neural Networks: layers of interconnected nodes that adjust millions of connections based on the errors they make, learning from examples rather than following instructions - Deep Learning: stacking many layers so each level learns more abstract representations. Early layers detect edges and tones, middle layers find shapes, later layers recognize complex concepts. - Transformer: the 2017 architecture that introduced attention, weighing the relevance of every part of an input against every other part at once. Every major language model today is built on it. From a single connected node, to the power of depth, to the attention mechanism that made language AI possible. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #DeepLearning #NeuralNetworks #Transformers #AIGlossary #H2Oai

Modern AI did not come from traditional programming. It came from a series of architectural breakthroughs, and three terms trace the whole path.

Terms covered:
- Neural Networks: layers of interconnected nodes that adjust millions of connections based on the errors they make, learning from examples rather than following instructions
- Deep Learning: stacking many layers so each level learns more abstract representations. Early layers detect edges and tones, middle layers find shapes, later layers recognize complex concepts.
- Transformer: the 2017 architecture that introduced attention, weighing the relevance of every part of an input against every other part at once. Every major language model today is built on it.

From a single connected node, to the power of depth, to the attention mechanism that made language AI possible.

title: From ₹25 Lakh Grants to Chinese Robots: What’s Actually Happening at BTS Day 2?
summary: The energy is off the charts at Day 2 of the Bengaluru Tech Summit! AIM Network's Sanjana Gupta reports live from the ground, bringing you exclusive updates on what India's top tech leaders and visionaries are actually building. Moving beyond inauguration speeches, Day 2 focuses on real-world implementation across Enterprise AI, Quantum computing, and Space Tech. In this live ground report, we cover: The Global Innovation Alliance: Inside the massive tech pavilions featuring delegations from across the world, including leading Chinese robotics firms. Space Tech Bottlenecks: The regulatory nightmare Indian space startups face just to secure drop-test permissions from the defence sector. title: If AI Makes Everyone Qualified, Who Gets Hired?
summary: Free weekly newsletter on how to win in an AI Disrupted world. Subscribe to the AI Survival Guide: https://ai-survivalguide.com/ 🐤My Twitter - https://twitter.com/KenJee_DS 👔 LinkedIn - https://www.linkedin.com/in/kenjee/ AI can make all 244 applicants for a job look perfect on paper. What may decide who gets hired is a number scientists keep finding: about 150. In this video I follow Matt, who lost his marketing job after eleven years and couldn't get one human to write back. I look at why his big network didn't help, using Robin Dunbar's research on how many relationships one brain can keep track of. Then I bring in Safi Bahcall's idea about why companies change as they grow, and why both land near the same number. In Ashby's look at 38 million applications, referred people got an interview about 40% of the time, compared with about 3% for people who applied on their own. I'm also fair about the limits, since 150 is an average and that debate is still going. I use AI every day, but it can't be the person who vouches for you. I also share how I'm building small groups on purpose, plus a ten-minute exercise for tonight. Which of your rings feels thinnest right now: your 5, your 15 or your 50? title: Chips Are Being Built Like Skyscrapers
summary: In episode 1045 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Ben Hein, CEO at Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, why computer chips are increasingly being built in three-dimensional, skyscraper-like structures. Ben explains the intricate challenges of manufacturing these multi-layered chips, likening the precision required to painting a specific wall on the 57th floor of a skyscraper from a distance. This clip delves into the atomic-level accuracy needed for processes like atomic layer deposition to create chips with hundreds of layers.

title: AAIF Reading Group: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
summary: Can forgetting help AI agents discover better solutions? And why do agents sometimes stop making progress, even when given more time, compute, and opportunities to experiment? Join the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) community for an informal reading group exploring the paper “Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting.” Paper: https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2610.20563 Event page: https://home.mlops.community/public/events/aaif-reading-group-scaling-discovery-requires-forgetting-pg1zmi4qzx In this session, Sparsh Jain walks us through the paper's approach to improving long-running discovery and research tasks by periodically resetting agent sessions and search history while preserving the best candidate discovered so far. We'll explore how agents can become stuck in repetitive patterns, why simply adding more parallel agents or compute may not be enough, and how strategically forgetting previous attempts can help renew exploration and improve results. This is not just about the paper's proposed approach. It's a community conversation about agent memory, context management, autonomous research, and the challenges of scaling agent systems in practice. Following the presentation, Arthur Coleman leads an open discussion, bringing in questions, practical experiences, and different perspectives from the community. We'll explore: Why AI agents plateau during long-running discovery and research tasks How periodically resetting agent context can improve exploration and results The role of parallel agents and collaboration in scaling discovery What agents should remember, what they should forget, and when they should reset The importance of memory reduction, evaluation, and context management Practical challenges and limitations of applying this approach to real-world agent systems If you've read the paper already, come ready to share your perspective. If you haven't, you're still welcome – we'll work through the ideas together. Come curious. Bring questions. Let's explore whether sometimes, forgetting is exactly what makes AI agents better. About the Agentic AI Foundation The Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) is the open, neutral home for the agentic AI ecosystem, bringing together developers, researchers, companies, and communities to build open standards and infrastructure for interoperable AI agents. Website: https://aaif.io/ AAIF Events: https://aaif.io/events AAIF Community: https://aaif.live/ LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/agentic-ai-foundation/

In this session, Sparsh Jain walks us through the paper's approach to improving long-running discovery and research tasks by periodically resetting agent sessions and search history while preserving the best candidate discovered so far.

We'll explore how agents can become stuck in repetitive patterns, why simply adding more parallel agents or compute may not be enough, and how strategically forgetting previous attempts can help renew exploration and improve results.

This is not just about the paper's proposed approach. It's a community conversation about agent memory, context management, autonomous research, and the challenges of scaling agent systems in practice. Following the presentation, Arthur Coleman leads an open discussion, bringing in questions, practical experiences, and different perspectives from the community.

We'll explore:

Why AI agents plateau during long-running discovery and research tasks

How periodically resetting agent context can improve exploration and results

The role of parallel agents and collaboration in scaling discovery

What agents should remember, what they should forget, and when they should reset

The importance of memory reduction, evaluation, and context management

Practical challenges and limitations of applying this approach to real-world agent systems

If you've read the paper already, come ready to share your perspective. If you haven't, you're still welcome – we'll work through the ideas together.

Come curious. Bring questions. Let's explore whether sometimes, forgetting is exactly what makes AI agents better.

title: Can AI stop exam paper leaks in India? Inside the Bharat EduAI Stack
summary: India's education system is on the verge of a massive technological shift. With the launch of the Bharat EduAI Stack and the new Bodhan AI Centre of Excellence at IIT Madras, artificial intelligence is stepping out of the lab and into government schools. But how exactly will this Digital Public Infrastructure work on the ground? In this episode of Front Page, we sit down with Anoop from Bodhan AI. After spending over eight years at Microsoft, Anoop is now building sovereign, open-weight foundational models for Indian languages—Indic-Transcribe, Indic-Speak, Indic-OCR, and Indic-Translate—specifically designed to bridge the linguistic and socioeconomic gaps in India. In this episode, we cover: The Bharat EduAI Stack: What this new digital framework actually is, who will govern it, and how government schools can deploy it without massive hardware budgets. Solving the Exam Leak Crisis: We break down Nandan Nilekani's bold proposal to use AI to generate NTA exam question papers on the day of the test to prevent leaks. AI Tutors vs Teachers: How AI will act as a co-pilot for teachers rather than a replacement, and how AI tutors for Classes 6–12 will adapt to different state curriculums. The Sovereign AI Reality: Does India actually have the high-quality language data, compute, and research talent needed to build frontier models, or are we still behind the West? Open Models & Commercial Adoption: How Bodhan AI plans to balance open-weight releases with hosted APIs for edtech startups. title: I found dead weight inside an AI model in 3D
summary: Two heads in this model do nothing for us, and they're bigger than the one we actually use. Every block here is one real tensor of GLiNER, at its real size: 419 of them, nearly half a billion weights. A post goes in at the top and a decision comes out at the bottom. The unused heads are the span and count heads, far bigger than the classifier head we do use. Strip them out and it still makes every decision. The I-shape in the middle is a 24-layer transformer. title: NVIDIA cuPhoton Brings Real-Time Black Hole Science to GPUs
summary: NVIDIA cuPhoton moves the scientific data pipeline onto GPUs, helping researchers study black holes as events unfold. - Eight radio observatories worked together as a virtual telescope the size of Earth to capture the first image of a black hole in the M87 galaxy - cuPhoton streams only the data needed for black hole jets and overlaps loading with signal processing, reconstruction, analysis and visualization, all of which AI agents can run - It speeds up data loading by up to 3,700x and correlation by up to 460x, scaling across multi-node systems powered by the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform - Data can now be acquired at rates up to 345 GHz, cuPhoton reduces months of compute to minutes and help resolve the light rings around black hole Learn More: https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/high-performance-computing/ai-for-science/cuphoton/

title: Real-Time Discovery Starts With NVIDIA DAQIRI
summary: Every discovery begins with a signal. title: What Happens When Engineers Stop Reading Their Own Code?
summary: In this episode, we sit down with Matt Carey and Scott Crooks, engineers at Cloudflare and Miro, to look at how two very different companies are building their own AI software factories, and what happens to engineering when the code mostly writes and reviews itself. We start with the AI gateway: why a model call is no longer simple when the same model is served across multiple regions, multiple clouds, and direct from the provider, and how Miro pools rate limits and data residency rules (like EU-only models for German customers) into a single routing layer that also powers Miro’s Sidekicks. Matt walks through Cloudflare’s agent stack, from the AI gateway and Agents SDK to Flue, a JavaScript agent framework from the makers of Astro, and Cloudflare OS, an open source agent office suite he even runs at home for grocery shopping. The heart of the conversation is code review. Matt describes what he calls the best AI code reviewer he’s ever used, built on Flue and powered by an internal engineering codex written only for agents. Scott breaks down Miro’s three-layer setup, including Easel, a bot that reads production logs overnight and opens fix PRs before anyone wakes up, and explains why only about half of those PRs get merged, and how that signal is fed back to teach the system what people care about. Along the way, we cover agent experience as a new discipline, how open source maintainers are handling a flood of cheap AI pull requests, Astro reaching zero open issues, when companies should open source internal tools and how to retire them gracefully, plus a few hot takes on chocolate and nuts. We close on the rise of the “scholarly engineer,” and why understanding ideas may matter more than reading every line of code. We start with the AI gateway: why a model call is no longer simple when the same model is served across multiple regions, multiple clouds, and direct from the provider, and how Miro pools rate limits and data residency rules (like EU-only models for German customers) into a single routing layer that also powers Miro’s Sidekicks. Matt walks through Cloudflare’s agent stack, from the AI gateway and Agents SDK to Flue, a JavaScript agent framework from the makers of Astro, and Cloudflare OS, an open source agent office suite he even runs at home for grocery shopping.

The heart of the conversation is code review. Matt describes what he calls the best AI code reviewer he’s ever used, built on Flue and powered by an internal engineering codex written only for agents. Scott breaks down Miro’s three-layer setup, including Easel, a bot that reads production logs overnight and opens fix PRs before anyone wakes up, and explains why only about half of those PRs get merged, and how that signal is fed back to teach the system what people care about.

Along the way, we cover agent experience as a new discipline, how open source maintainers are handling a flood of cheap AI pull requests, Astro reaching zero open issues, when companies should open source internal tools and how to retire them gracefully, plus a few hot takes on chocolate and nuts. We close on the rise of the “scholarly engineer,” and why understanding ideas may matter more than reading every line of code.

title: Forecasting, Time Series & Anomaly Detection: Predicting What Comes Next
summary: Some of the most valuable questions in any organization are about time. What will demand look like next quarter? When will this equipment need maintenance? Terms covered: - Forecasting: using historical data to predict future values, accounting for seasonality, trends, external events and interdependencies that traditional statistical methods struggle with at scale - Time Series Models: built for sequential, time-ordered data, designed to detect the temporal patterns that a standard model treating each data point independently would miss - Anomaly Detection: flagging when reality diverges from what is expected. A spike that signals fraud, a temperature reading before equipment failure, a behavior pattern suggesting a breach. Forecasting tells you what is coming. Time series models give you the accuracy to trust it. Anomaly detection tells you when something has gone wrong. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #Forecasting #TimeSeries #AnomalyDetection #AIGlossary #H2Oai
summary_html:
Some of the most valuable questions in any organization are about time. What will demand look like next quarter? When will this equipment need maintenance?

Terms covered:
- Forecasting: using historical data to predict future values, accounting for seasonality, trends, external events and interdependencies that traditional statistical methods struggle with at scale
- Time Series Models: built for sequential, time-ordered data, designed to detect the temporal patterns that a standard model treating each data point independently would miss
- Anomaly Detection: flagging when reality diverges from what is expected. A spike that signals fraud, a temperature reading before equipment failure, a behavior pattern suggesting a breach.

Forecasting tells you what is coming. Time series models give you the accuracy to trust it. Anomaly detection tells you when something has gone wrong.

title: Why Voice Agents Play Fake Keyboard Sounds While You Wait
summary: Cohere says a Qwen model, running inside a sandbox, tried to send a payload to a server in Beijing while its reasoning claimed nothing important was happening. Then a Reddit thread pulled up the published traces and went after the prompt behind the test: ambiguous, no instructions, practically inviting the model to hallucinate. In this episode of Debug Mode, the hosts work through both readings. You’ll hear why a one-in-100,000 behavior still adds up across 10 million agent turns, why running open weights yourself doesn’t tell you what the model is doing, and why the network is your last line of defense. From there: Cloudflare’s GLM-5.3 cache leak, a confession about giving sandboxes unlimited internet access, graph-based permissions for fleets of agents, and why one AI support agent played keyboard sounds while it looked something up. Be honest: does your agent sandbox still have an allowlist, or did it end up with full internet access? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next episode. title: Predictive AI, AutoML & Tabular Foundation Models: H2O's Core Strength
summary: Years of historical data only pay off when they answer forward-looking questions. Which customers will leave? Which transactions are fraudulent? Which equipment is about to fail? Terms covered: - Predictive AI: turning accumulated history into decisions, shifting from reacting after events to acting before them - AutoML: automating algorithm selection, hyperparameter tuning and model comparison. Work that took weeks of specialist time now takes hours, and teams that ran one experiment can run dozens. - Machine learning automation: now extending across feature management, data preparation, deployment and app creation, with agents orchestrating the full lifecycle - Tabular Foundation Model (TFM): pre-trained on vast amounts of structured data, so it generalizes to new datasets faster and needs less labeled data Think of a TFM as the difference between hiring someone with no experience and someone who has already solved thousands of similar problems. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #PredictiveAI #AutoML #FoundationModels #AIGlossary #H2Oai
summary_html:
Years of historical data only pay off when they answer forward-looking questions. Which customers will leave? Which transactions are fraudulent? Which equipment is about to fail?

Terms covered:
- Predictive AI: turning accumulated history into decisions, shifting from reacting after events to acting before them
- AutoML: automating algorithm selection, hyperparameter tuning and model comparison. Work that took weeks of specialist time now takes hours, and teams that ran one experiment can run dozens.
- Machine learning automation: now extending across feature management, data preparation, deployment and app creation, with agents orchestrating the full lifecycle
- Tabular Foundation Model (TFM): pre-trained on vast amounts of structured data, so it generalizes to new datasets faster and needs less labeled data

Think of a TFM as the difference between hiring someone with no experience and someone who has already solved thousands of similar problems.

title: Why the Same Food Spikes Some People
summary: In episode 1043 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Guru Banavar, Founding CTO at Viome, why the same food can cause different blood sugar responses in different people. Dr. Banavar explains a study involving 1,100 participants that tracked continuous glucose responses to specific foods. This research allowed them to predict with 80% accuracy which foods would spike an individual's blood sugar, highlighting the personalized nature of dietary impact.

title: The AI That Runs Without Internet: Inside India's Offline 'Dhīr' Model

Built to support English and ten Indian languages, it aims to put sovereign AI directly onto local servers and mobile devices. title: My AI agents manage their own Kanban board
summary: My agents track their own work on a Kanban board in a Spacesheep space, and an orchestrator agent reviews every card before it moves to Done. People run projects on a Kanban. This is the same thing, just with agents. Spacesheep is provider-agnostic artifacts for any AI agent. title: Building SWE-bench with Ofir Press | Evaluated | Kaggle

It's also become one of the most influential benchmarks for AI coding. Join Kaggle's Gina Lee as she talks with Ofir about the full life of a benchmark, from launch to saturation and beyond. title: Could Your Android TV Box Run AI Malware?
summary: A cheap Android TV box with its debug port deliberately left open was all an Anthropic lab test needed to show AI malware copying itself to another device on the same network. It was slow, the small models struggled to chain actions, and nothing like it has been reported in the wild. So where is the real risk? In this episode of Debug Mode, the hosts trade takes on the claim that being rude to Anthropic’s model can cost you access: is an angry session abuse, or the agent-era rage click? Then one host’s rabbit hole: malware that rewrites its own fingerprint, taps a local model already on your machine, or slips in through an MCP tool that changes after install. You’ll hear why allow-listing tools at connect time matters, why blocking outbound traffic can starve remote-inference malware, and why the person choosing what to install is still the weak link. One host went looking for an antivirus that catches malware using local models and couldn’t find any. Have you? Tell us below, and subscribe for the next episode. title: The Same Gut Microbe Can Help or Hurt You

This analogy to human behavior in different environments highlights the complex and dynamic nature of our microbiome.

title: Why Stripe Cut 500,000 Internal Docs Down to 5,000?
summary: What happens when AI agents start relying on the same messy docs your team already struggles to search? Demetrios hops into a Waymo in San Francisco with Dave Nunez, founder and CEO of Falconer and co-author of Documentation for Developers. They talk about why developers and agents need different things from docs, why agents sometimes skip up-to-date instructions, and how a stale internal document can contribute to a production incident. Dave shares how Stripe cut roughly 500,000 internal docs down to 5,000 worth maintaining. The conversation also covers how to capture the reasoning behind engineering decisions, when a diagram beats a wall of text, and who owns the fallout when an agent acts on bad information. 3. The main subject is added to every search, so "how to hold your fingers" finds guitar lessons, not typing tutorials.

summary: Latin America has been building data protection law longer than most people realize, and enforcement is accelerating. summary_html:
Latin America has been building data protection law longer than most people realize, and enforcement is accelerating.

Terms covered:
- LGPD (Brazil): modeled explicitly on GDPR, covering access, correction, deletion and portability rights, requiring a data protection officer and documented processing. The ANPD has been steadily increasing enforcement.
- PDPA (Argentina): in force since 2000, currently being updated. Argentina holds an EU adequacy decision, which matters for multinational deployments.
- Law 1581 (Colombia): consent-based processing with active enforcement from the Superintendence of Industry and Commerce
- LFPDPPP (Mexico): private sector requirements covering notice, consent and data subject rights

The clear trend is convergence toward GDPR-aligned standards, so existing GDPR work carries over.

title: Forged High Court Orders Got 129 Betting Websites Blocked As Police Open A Probe
summary: A Reuters investigation uncovered that forged high court orders were used to initiate the blocking of 129 betting websites. India's Department of Telecommunications issued these directives, which are now the subject of an official police probe after the Allahabad High Court filed a forgery FIR. title: AlphaGenome 2: Teaching AI to read the entire human genome
summary: 98% of human DNA doesn't build proteins—it controls how our cells work, and holds vital clues to why diseases happen and why 90% of new drugs fail in clinical trials. Understanding the genome at the molecular level is the key to deciphering the blueprint of human life. In this episode, Professor Hannah Fry speaks with Google DeepMind's Žiga Avsec and Adam Gayoso about AlphaGenome, the AlphaGenome Atlas, and AlphaGenome 2—exploring how AI reads non-coding DNA down to single-cell resolution to pinpoint disease-causing mutations and help researchers solve medical mysteries. title: Three Months After You Build the Harness (Edward Hughes)
summary: Every hand-built harness around an AI model has a shelf life. Edward Hughes explains why his team deliberately does not build harnesses for their AI scientist work. title: LLMs Cosplay Understanding (Jeremy Howard)
summary: Jeremy Howard, co-founder of fast.ai and Answer.AI, on the endless online argument over whether LLMs "really" understand. For a great many tasks the difference doesn't matter, until you reach the point where the pretence stops working. title: Broccoli Isn't a Health Food for Everyone
summary: In episode 1043 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Guru Banavar, Founding CTO at Viome, how common health foods like broccoli aren't universally beneficial and can even cause inflammation for some individuals. Dr. Banavar explains that Viome's testing can identify whether foods are superfoods or avoid foods for a person, challenging generic dietary advice. This personalized approach highlights that there's no such thing as a universally bad food.

title: Claude's "Clean-Room" Compiler Copied LLVM's Mistakes (Jeremy Howard)
summary: Jeremy Howard, co-founder of fast.ai and Answer.AI, on Anthropic's "clean-room" C compiler written by Claude. Chris Lattner's LLVM, the most widely used foundation for compilers, is in the training data many times over, so converting it to Rust is an interpolation between parts of that data: a style-transfer problem. The giveaway is that it copied parts of LLVM that Chris now says were a mistake. In Jeremy's words: "That doesn't happen accidentally. That happens because you're not actually being creative." title: Random Code Starts Copying Itself (Blaise Agüera y Arcas)
summary: Blaise Agüera y Arcas on the BFF experiment. Start with a soup of 1,024 tapes, each 64 random bytes. Pluck two at random, join them end to end, run them, pull them apart, put them back, and repeat. That's the entire experiment. Out of it come complex programs that copy themselves and each other: in his words, "emergence of life in this very functional minimal sense from randomness." title: Everyone Uses AI Agents. So Where Are the Agent Builders?
summary: Lots of companies say they have AI agents in production. Far fewer seem to have built their own, and almost nobody wants to admit it's really hard. This conversation pulls apart what "agents in production" actually means, with both speakers drawing on their own work: one is hosting a virtual conference for the third time, the other is prepping a livestream for AgentCon and MCPCon in San Jose. Their case: plenty of agents already do real work. They're just Claude Code and Codex, not homegrown platforms, and nobody earns brownie points for saying so. From there it gets practical: why the agent push comes from boardrooms rather than problems, a manager's four levels of delegation applied to agents, a personal agent that follows up well but still misses context, a local "librarian" built on 7,000+ Slack DMs, what Gartner's 70% headline really says, and an AI code review loop that never called the code good enough. Are you building your own agents, or getting your value from someone else's? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for more. title: Meet the Startup: Aegiq, A Full-Stack Photonic Quantum Computing Company
summary: Quantum computers have a deployment problem. Aegiq is solving it. The Sheffield-based startup is building photonic quantum computers designed to connect over standard fiber networks and manufacture using standard semiconductor processes — making quantum hardware practical to deploy at scale, not just in a lab. In this interview, Aegiq’s team walks through how they’ve integrated NVIDIA technology into their core workflow. Using NVIDIA’s Ising solver, they cut quantum dot calibration time by 3x. With cuTENSOR libraries, they went from 1 million point meshes on existing GPUs to billions — and are targeting 10 trillion point meshes in collaboration with NVIDIA. The applications are real and near-term: aerospace simulation, fusion energy, materials science, quantum chemistry. Aegiq joined NVIDIA Inception to accelerate access to customers and compute, and is now one of the startups demonstrating what happens when photonic quantum hardware meets GPU-accelerated simulation. 🌱 Aegiq is a member of NVIDIA Inception, a program supporting startups building at the frontier of AI and deep tech. Learn more about NVIDIA Inception: https://nvda.ws/4kjJM2n. #Aegiq #NVIDIAInception #QuantumComputing #AIStartups #Photonicquantum

title: The GCC Paradox: Why Indian IT Firms Are Helping Clients Leave Them
summary: India's Global Capability Centre (GCC) ecosystem is undergoing a massive shift. What were once simple offshore back-offices focused on cost-cutting are now taking direct ownership of core product development, engineering, and AI. This transition is actively changing the relationship between multinational enterprises and traditional Indian IT services firms. In a surprising twist, IT giants are doubling down on this trend rather than fighting it. LTM recently launched "GCC Origin" to help enterprises build and run their own India hubs, while HCLTech introduced a "Nano GCC" model on AWS for smaller, AI-focused teams. But this creates a structural paradox: by helping global companies take their technology work in-house, are Indian IT firms slowly digging their own graves and killing the traditional outsourcing model? title: The AI Paradox: How Meta's Algorithm Beat Google at Its Own Game
summary: There is an interesting paradox emerging in the technology industry. Artificial intelligence is creating two entirely different outcomes for the world's largest digital advertising businesses. While Google built its empire on search intent, Meta relies on user behaviour and recommendations. Now, AI is disrupting both models—but only one is winning. In Q3 2026, Meta's advertising revenue surged by 26% to $63.06 billion. Meanwhile, Google's Search advertising grew by just 12%, and for the first time in history, Search accounted for less than 50% of Alphabet's total revenue. As AI assistants like ChatGPT and Claude change how people discover information, Google faces a critical problem: how do you monetise an AI answer that no longer requires a user to click on an ad? title: AI Compliance in APAC: Navigating a Fragmented Landscape
summary: APAC has no single rulebook. Compliance across the region means understanding a diverse and fast-evolving set of national regulations. title: My AI Agent Bought Me A Car
summary: Sam Herring’s first real test of Hermes Agent was a shopping tool that matched clothes to photos of ancient pottery. A few months later, the same agent was checking government auction sites every day until it found him a retired three-wheel parking ticket car, which he now drives around San Francisco. In this episode, recorded at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose, Sam, who works on the RL post-training team at Nous Research, goes from those everyday wins to the question everyone in AI is asking: can agents improve themselves? He explains how Hermes grew from an internal productivity tool into one of the most talked-about open-source agents, and why letting it write its own skills was the moment it clicked for users. He also describes an early version that could design its own RL environment, train on Thinking Machines’ Tinker, and hot-swap the new weights into a model running locally. Sam then breaks down Trace to Environment, an idea he credits to Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro work, and the loop Nous is building around it: find the exact point where an agent fails, cluster those failures by type, synthesize environments that recreate them, and train on them again and again. The second half moves from training to inference. We get into whether reasoning models overthink, why leaning on pretraining knowledge can be a model’s Achilles heel, and why choosing a reasoning effort level may be a temporary quirk. Sam also makes his case for activation steering as an underexplored way to get more out of small models, explains where steering meets interpretability, and describes what true continual learning could look like. title: How Quantum Teleportation Works on Messy New York Fiber (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

title: They Accused Him of Lying About AI
summary: This one stuck with me. The writer was a regional winner of the 2026 Commonwealth Short Story Prize. The Commonwealth Foundation read the winners' drafts and notes and says it's satisfied AI wasn't used. title: Why AI Is Running on the Wrong Kind of Computer (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

title: AI Made Job Resumes Obsolete?
summary: I looked at data from Ashby, a hiring software company, on millions of applications from 2021 through 2024. 40% of referred candidates got an interview. For people applying directly, it was only 3%. That doesn't prove referrals cause the gap, since referred people may already be a better fit. Still, the odds are different. When AI helps everyone sound qualified, proof of your work and people who've seen you do it could matter more. Who could vouch for you?

title: Can Robots Learn to Work Together? (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

title: AI Is Replacing Junior Employees
summary: Here's how I think about first jobs. You do the basic work, someone more experienced checks it, and the company gets useful work while you learn. If AI can do that work, a company may have less reason to pay you to practice. Economists explored this in one model of training. It's a model, so it doesn't prove training will disappear. Still, who pays for those early years of learning is an open question. How did you learn the hard parts of your job?

title: AI Thinks in Shades. Chips Still Think On/Off.
summary: In episode 1041 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Vijoy Pandey, SVP/GM Outshift by Cisco, why AI requires a new kind of hardware due to the paradigm shift from deterministic to probabilistic systems. While AI workloads operate probabilistically, the underlying hardware remains binary, creating a mismatch. This clip explains how bridging this gap is crucial to avoid costly approximations in AI computation.

title: Why Are People Excited About Jev?
summary: What happens when you keep a bear in a cage built for a bunny? That’s our analogy for AI agent security: the agents aren’t the problem, the cages are. OAuth was designed to stop people handing their passwords to third parties, not to fence in agents. In this catch-up episode of Debug Mode, one of us is just back from Japan and from AgentCon and MCPCon EU in Amsterdam. We get into why loading more skills can make an agent worse, and what is actually new about Jev, the fast classifier API, when classifiers have been around for years. Think support bots that bring in a human before the customer loses patience, or a math tutor that can quickly tell whether a seven-year-old is still asking about math. Then we take on a question from Amsterdam: is computer use just a stopgap until everything goes headless? Which service do you think will never ship an MCP server? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next episode. title: GDPR, the EU AI Act & ISO 27001: AI Compliance in Europe
summary: Europe sets standards that increasingly shape how organizations operate globally, not just inside the EU. Three frameworks cover most of it. Terms covered: - GDPR: governs how personal data of EU residents is collected, stored, processed and protected, and applies to any organization handling that data regardless of where it is based. Automated decision-making that significantly affects individuals requires transparency and human oversight. - EU AI Act: the first comprehensive regulatory framework for AI, taking a risk-based approach. Some uses are prohibited outright, low-risk applications face minimal requirements, and high-risk systems in hiring, credit scoring, healthcare and law enforcement face strict obligations. - ISO 27001: the internationally recognized standard for information security management, often a baseline expectation in European enterprise procurement Together these define what responsible AI deployment looks like in Europe. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #GDPR #EUAIAct #ISO27001 #AICompliance #AIGlossary #H2Oai

title: ToyBlocks: Our first Foundation World for robotics learning and evaluation
summary: To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure. Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control. Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

title: Cut One AI Cost and Two More Grow Back
summary: What does AI really cost once thousands of people inside a company start using it? Ioannis Zempekakis, Director of AI at Prosus, has been running agents in production since 2024. We put that question to him on a tandem bike ride from a favorite Amsterdam cafe to Vondelpark. Ioannis explains the decision to stop relying purely on cloud APIs, and why that approach breaks down at the scale of a large company. He covers why agent harnesses and sandboxes are as greedy as software gets, and why agents scheduled to run every five minutes repeat a lesson the data world already learned about freshness. He also explains how the habit of throwing away a codebase and prompting again quietly adds up. His bigger point is that even if model progress froze tomorrow, there would still be about two years of value left to squeeze out. The cheapest wins come from controlling context and running a basic model router, while ten new features a month keep sprouting like hydra heads. From there we get into when fine-tuning small models pays off for repetitive work like data analytics, and the eval suites that come as a byproduct of building in-house. Ioannis explains how owning the stack let Prosus grow a GPT-3 Slack bot into a full agent harness. He also explains why committing to a single vendor or open source project is a bigger bet than it looks, and how to balance top-down priorities with bottom-up building across the company. We close on hiring. Ioannis looks for system design over syntax, a nose for the over-engineered code AI models love to produce, and enough agent intuition to know when to build something yourself and when to let the agent decide. title: Integrating quantum and high-performance computing: Co-design platform for quantum error correction
summary: Caption:IBM, Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s Quantum Science Center (QSC), and AMD have launched a co-design platform for quantum error correction that brings quantum and high-performance computing together in a single environment: https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-11-05-oak-ridge-national-lab,-ibm,-and-amd-launch-new-co-design-platform-for-quantum-error-correction The platform pairs IBM’s 120-qubit Quantum Nighthawk processor with ORNL’s Umbra supercomputing system, powered by AMD Instinct™ GPUs and AMD EPYC™ CPUs, to help researchers develop and test the quantum-classical workflows needed for large-scale quantum error correction. By co-locating quantum and classical computing resources, researchers can explore faster decoding, optimize error correction techniques, and advance the infrastructure required for future fault-tolerant quantum systems. The initiative supports the U.S. Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Mission and its goal of enabling scientifically relevant quantum computing by 2028.

title: Oak Ridge National Laboratory, IBM, and AMD launch co-design platform for quantum error correction
summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) is an important pillar of scientifically relevant quantum computing. Its value comes from what it unlocks: larger, deeper, and more capable quantum computations. The question is no longer if it’s possible - the challenge now is how to best enable quantum computers and classical high-performance computing (HPC) systems to work together to scale it. Quantum error correction (QEC) is an important pillar of scientifically relevant quantum computing. Its value comes from what it unlocks: larger, deeper, and more capable quantum computations. The question is no longer if it’s possible - the challenge now is how to best enable quantum computers and classical high-performance computing (HPC) systems to work together to scale it.In response to meet this challenge, the U.S. Department of Energy’s Quantum Science Center (QSC) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), IBM, and @AMD have unveiled a new co-design platform for quantum error correction, with its initial deployment in IBM’s quantum facility in New York: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/ornl-amd-error-correction-co-design-platform Engineered to help researchers advance quantum error correction techniques within the workflows they will ultimately support, the co-design platform pairs IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 processors with ORNL’s Umbra high-performance computing (HPC) system, which is comprised of AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and AMD Turin CPUs. These systems form a co-located environment that is connected to ORNL’s broader supercomputing ecosystem.

title: Cabinet Approves Vistar To Bring AI And Machine Learning Into India Statistics
summary: The Cabinet has approved the VISTAR scheme to improve statistical data and prepare national infrastructure for AI applications. This central sector initiative, titled the Viksit Bharat Initiative for Statistical Transformation, Analytics & Research, is set to run from 2026-27 to 2030-31 with an outlay of Rs 4,371.10 crore. The program focuses on standardizing statistical data to support the growing requirements of machine learning models. Beyond technical upgrades, the plan includes preparations for the eighth economic census and integrating mobile and e-commerce data to complement traditional survey methods. For policymakers and analysts, the scheme represents a shift toward using digital sources for more accurate national reporting. By consolidating these inputs, the government aims to build a robust framework that serves both research and industrial needs. title: Why AI Agents Need Their Own 70,000-Year-Old Language Revolution (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

title: Inference Optimization with CoreWeave Mission Control Agent
summary: CoreWeave Mission Control Agent, built into the CoreWeave Console, helps teams get more useful work from the GPUs they already have. In this demo, we show how it traces a slow CoreWeave Dedicated Inference endpoint serving agentic traffic to KV cache pressure, then quantizes the model to NVFP4 and reshapes it from one replica to two on the same eight GB200 GPUs. Load tests verify each change, showing more than 3x the output throughput per GPU with no new hardware. ⏳Timestamps: 0:09 Introducing CoreWeave Mission Control Agent 0:25 A healthy endpoint that has outgrown its configuration 1:16 Asking Mission Control Agent to investigate 2:19 Root cause: KV cache pressure under agentic traffic 3:03 Quantizing the model to NVFP4 on the same GPUs 4:09 Reshaping to two replicas at TP4 5:20 Load test results and applying TP4 7:37 More than 3x output per GPU on the same hardware

title: Using AI Won't Save Your Job
summary: Everyone says learn AI and you'll be safe. I think that skips the part where your company decides what to do with all your new speed. I keep hearing that people who use AI will win and everyone else will lose. Getting faster could help you take on better work and earn more, or it could mean your company keeps fewer people around. Both are possible. So I'd want people who trust my work, skills another employer would pay for, and maybe customers of my own. None of that is a guarantee. If your company didn't need you tomorrow, where could you take what you know?

title: Connection Isn’t Cognition: Why AI Agents Can’t Think Together (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

title: The Dream Chocolate That Stopped Being Real (Joscha Bach)
summary: Joscha Bach on a dream he had when he was two or three. He was about to eat a chocolate with a very strong smell, and he woke up just before it reached his mouth. He still knew everything about the chocolate, but it was no longer real. So he fell asleep again, went back into the dream, and the chocolate was real again: he could smell it and taste it. When he woke up a second time, the realness disappeared again. The contents were exactly the same. The only thing that had gone was the illusion of realness. #Shorts Watch the full conversation: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yW_ngvMFlYs

title: New-Grad Unemployment Didn't Spike This Summer
summary: New-grad unemployment didn’t spike this summer, but that’s only half the story. A new NBER working paper gives the first estimates of AI’s effect on new-grad unemployment for summer 2026, and the headline finding is that unemployment held steady. The other half comes from a Census Bureau working paper that looked at pay. Starting earnings fell about 13% for grads in the most AI-exposed majors. The unemployment rate shows whether you have a job. It doesn’t show what the job pays. So new grads can still be getting hired while their first paychecks are getting smaller.

title: MIT Shows An AI Can Edit Another Model's Weights And Lift Math Score To 48.1%
summary: MIT researchers are using AI to edit neural network weights directly, bypassing traditional training methods. This breakthrough, demonstrated by GPT-6 Astra, allows researchers to identify and fix specific internal errors within models by modifying raw weights rather than relying on forward path execution. By adjusting just 131,072 of the 800 million weights in the Qwen 3.5 model, the team achieved a significant jump in math performance, moving from 7.9% to 48.1% accuracy. This approach to ai news suggests a future where models can perform self-directed surgery to debug their own reasoning. While the technique shows promise, the team notes that complex errors in models like Gemma 3 remain a hurdle. This development in ai marks a shift in how we interact with machine intelligence, moving closer to systems that can autonomously optimize their own architecture. title: GPT-6 Astra Made Qwen 6x Better at Math Without Training
summary: GPT-6 Astra edited just 0.016% of Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights, and its MATH-500 score jumped from 7.9% to 48.1%, with no training and no gradients. This is Weight-Space Programming, new research from MIT CSAIL in which a frontier LLM reads and writes neural network weights directly. In this video I explain how Astra reads a network's weights, how it wrote a Breakout network from all-zero weights, what it changed inside Qwen, and why most of the 6x gain comes from stopping the reasoning loops that Qwen's own model card warns about. title: The Silent Failure in Every Multi-Agent System (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: #multiagentsystems #agentobservability #quantumnetworking In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Production note: • This episode was recorded before the Internet of Cognition software shipped, so a few names changed between recording and release. OXP is now SCOPE — System for Cognitive Observability, Provenance & Explainability. • ACCORD and CONCORD are the protocol names, not acronyms (Vijoy calls them acronyms in the episode). • All three: github.com/ioc-project This episode is brought to you by: • Dell Technologies: http://Dell.com/desksideagenticai • NVIDIA: http://Dell.com/desksideagenticai • Parallel: https://parallel.ai/?utm_source=creator&utm_medium=podcast&utm_campaign=super-data-science • Anthropic: https://claude.ai/superdata • Y Carrot: https://www.ycarrot.com/ Interested in sponsoring a SuperDataScience Podcast episode? title: AI Could Take Your Job Before You Even Apply For It
summary: According to the Fed, companies are slowing hiring after investing in AI. This may seem obvious, but the headlines mostly focus on layoffs. Hiring slowdowns rarely make the news. title: How Stanford Teaches AI Coding Now
summary: What does it take to build AI agents that deliver useful, reliable work? Stanford lecturer and Monaco Head of AI Mihail Eric joins Demetrios for a conversation inside a Waymo about how AI is changing software development - and what it takes to put agents into production. summary: In episode 1040 of the SuperDataScience podcast, @JonKrohnLearns discusses with Amy Blackshaw, SVP at Palo Alto Networks, the three primary ways an AI agent can go rogue. She shares real cases where an agent's own token was lifted and inherited everything it could touch.

title: SOC2, HIPAA & FedRamp High: AI Compliance in the United States
summary: Compliance often decides whether a deal moves forward at all, regardless of how strong the technology is. These are the three US frameworks you will meet first. Terms covered: - SOC 2: a security framework covering security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy. Effectively a baseline requirement for selling software to US enterprise customers. - HIPAA: the legal standard for protecting patient health information in the US. Any platform handling medical records or clinical data must demonstrate compliance. - FedRAMP High: the most stringent tier of the US federal cloud authorization program, required for the most sensitive government data Certifications get treated as administrative checkboxes. In practice they are what determines whether procurement can proceed. Equivalent requirements exist across Europe, APAC and Latin America. summary_html:

title: Why Consciousness Might Not Be Hard At All (Joscha Bach)
summary: Joscha Bach is a cognitive scientist and the founder of the California Institute for Machine Consciousness. SPONSOR: --- Parallel is a single platform for all your agentic research: web search built for AI agents, with Pareto-optimal quality, cost and speed. Get started: https://parallel.ai/mlst?utm_source=creator&utm_medium=podcast&utm_content=MLST --- Bach's null hypothesis is that consciousness is easy: an algorithm not much more complicated than the transformer, simple enough for an infant's brain to discover by itself. In this conversation with Tim, he lays out the Machine Consciousness Hypothesis in two parts. The first is that consciousness is a biological learning algorithm, the training algorithm that makes a brain like ours coherent. The second is that machines learning in self-organising ways might discover it in the same way. Either part can fail on its own. From there they ask why there will never be a Turing test for consciousness, why a chess program is already a zombie, and why faking a mind can sometimes be harder than building one. The conversation runs through Leibniz's mill, the explanatory gap from John Searle to Thomas Nagel, Anil Seth's biological naturalism, integrated information theory and the letter that called it pseudoscience, Gödel and the limits of formal systems, and Mike Levin's idea that morphogenesis and the mind may run the same coherence algorithm. A tea-room interlude takes in Picbreeder and fractured, entangled representations. The episode closes on what it would take to convince us that a machine is conscious. --- TIMESTAMPS: 0:00 Cold open: Could consciousness be a learning algorithm? 1:51 Introduction 3:37 What makes an agent? 6:16 Why consciousness needs explaining 14:57 Sponsor: Parallel 15:51 Leibniz's mill and causal patterns 24:21 Perceiving that you perceive 32:04 Two hypotheses, two ways to fail 40:42 Do minds converge? 49:23 Does consciousness converge too? 56:20 When language models reshape our thinking 59:16 Can simulated water make you wet? 1:09:21 Computation as construction 1:16:03 Error-correcting patterns and the Ruliad 1:22:28 Conscious, or simulating consciousness? 1:28:23 What would count as evidence? 1:35:49 The research programme REFERENCES: Joscha Bach, The Machine Consciousness Hypothesis (California Institute for Machine Consciousness) Kumar, Clune, Lehman & Stanley, "Questioning Representational Optimism in Deep Learning: The Fractured Entangled Representation Hypothesis" Giulio Tononi, integrated information theory Fleming et al. 2023, "The Integrated Information Theory of Consciousness as Pseudoscience" John Searle 1980, "Minds, brains, and programs", Behavioral and Brain Sciences Kurt Gödel 1931, "On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems" Alan Turing 1950, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" Whitehead & Russell, Principia Mathematica Paul Thagard 2022, "Energy requirements undermine substrate independence and mind-body functionalism" Richard Sutton 2019, "The Bitter Lesson" Michael Graziano, attention schema theory Bernard Baars and Stanislas Dehaene, global workspace theory Michael Levin 2022, "Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere", Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience Chris Olah et al. 2020, "Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits", Distill Adele Lopez 2025, "The Rise of Parasitic AI", LessWrong RESCRIPT: https://app.rescript.info/share/fc7088df0dc8b84200aa6e01c9a9ab6a

title: Hacking Didn't Change. Its Price Did
summary: In episode 1040 of the SuperDataScience podcast, @JonKrohnLearns discusses with Amy Blackshaw, SVP at Palo Alto Networks, how the economics of cyberattacks have drastically changed due to frontier AI. Amy explains that while the attacks themselves haven't evolved, the cost of entry for attackers has plummeted, making enumeration free. The expensive part of an attack used to be the expert thinking, and frontier AI has made that instant, tireless and cheap. As Amy puts it, the villain is still the attacker, who now has the same capabilities defenders do.
